title: ROMANS 1 ALSO DESCRIBES MEN BURNING WITH PASSION FOR OTHER MEN—Why Is This Passage So Debated?
paragraphs: ROMANS 1 ALSO DESCRIBES MEN BURNING WITH PASSION FOR OTHER MEN—Why Is This Passage So Debated?

Romans 1:27 says something our generation keeps arguing about. But before you use this verse against someone else, you need to hear what Paul says next—because Romans 1 was never written to give religious people permission to stand above sinners. It was written to bring the whole human race to its knees before the mercy of Jesus Christ.
There are Bible verses people whisper about.
Verses people weaponize.
Verses people avoid because they are afraid of what their friends will think if they believe them.
And then there are verses like Romans 1:27.
Read at a distance, it can become ammunition.
Read carelessly, it can become cruelty.
Ignored completely, it can become another place where Christians quietly decide that modern culture has greater authority than Scripture.
But read in context—slowly, humbly, with Romans 2 and Romans 3 still waiting ahead of us—it becomes something much more unsettling.
Because Paul is not merely talking about them.
Eventually, Paul is coming for all of us.
And that changes everything.
The New Testament was written in Greek, not English, so before debating what Romans 1:27 means, we should at least listen to some of the language Paul actually used:
“οἱ ἄρσενες… ἐξεκαύθησαν ἐν τῇ ὀρέξει αὐτῶν εἰς ἀλλήλους, ἄρσενες ἐν ἄρσεσιν…”
hoi arsenes… exekauthēsan en tē orexei autōn eis allēlous, arsenes en arsenesin…

The language describes males abandoning sexual relations with females and becoming inflamed in desire toward one another—“males with males.” That basic observation is not created by an English translation; it is present in the Greek itself.
One word is especially vivid.
ἐξεκαύθησαν — exekauthēsan.
It carries the imagery of being kindled, inflamed, burning.
And Paul says the desire is εἰς ἀλλήλους — eis allēlous: toward one another.
Then comes the striking expression ἄρσενες ἐν ἄρσεσιν — arsenes en arsenesin: males with males.
So we should not pretend Romans 1:27 says nothing about male same-sex sexual behavior.
It does.

That does not settle every modern question about sexual orientation, psychology, pastoral care, temptation, identity, civil law, or how Christians should speak to LGBTQ people. Paul was writing in the first-century Greco-Roman world, not answering a twenty-first-century questionnaire about every dimension of sexuality.
But neither should historical distance become an excuse for making Paul's actual words disappear.
This is one reason the passage remains so fiercely debated.

Some interpreters have argued that Paul's condemnation should be understood more narrowly against particular ancient practices or cultural circumstances. Others understand Romans 1:26–27 as a general rejection of same-sex sexual relations within Paul's larger Jewish-Christian sexual ethic. The debate involves questions about ancient sexuality, Paul's use of “nature,” the relationship between desire and conduct, and how Paul's argument should be applied today.
Yet whatever disagreements surround its application, the Greek of verse 27 explicitly depicts males desiring other males and engaging in sexual behavior with males.
But now comes the part that is often missed.
Romans 1 did not begin with homosexuality.
It began with worship.
That changes the entire conversation.
Paul's deeper diagnosis appears in Romans 1:25: humanity exchanged God's truth for a lie and worshiped and served created things rather than the Creator.
Before Paul talks about disordered sexuality, he talks about disordered worship.
Before he describes what human beings do with their bodies, he describes what human beings have done with God.
That means the deepest crisis in Romans 1 is not simply, “Some people experience sinful sexual desires.”
The deeper tragedy is:
The creature has taken the Creator's throne.
And suddenly this chapter becomes dangerously personal.
Because you may never have desired another person of the same sex…
but you can worship money.
You can worship approval.
You can worship your reputation.
You can worship your career.
You can worship romance.
You can worship political power.
You can worship pornography.
You can worship your body.
You can worship your church position.
You can even worship the image of yourself as the person who is morally superior to everybody mentioned in Romans 1.
Anything created can become an idol when it occupies the place belonging to the Creator.
And that is why Romans 1 is much bigger than one sexual controversy.
Keep reading.
Paul's catalogue expands into greed, envy, murder, strife, deceit, malice, gossip, slander, arrogance, boastfulness, disobedience to parents, faithlessness and mercilessness.
That list should make the smug Christian uncomfortable.
Imagine holding Romans 1:27 like a spotlight pointed at somebody else's bedroom while quietly stepping over Romans 1:29–31 as though those verses belonged to somebody else.
Paul will not permit it.
And then Romans 2 begins.
This may be one of the most important chapter turns in the entire conversation.
The person listening to Paul's indictment might have been nodding.
“Yes.”
“Exactly.”
“Look how sinful those people are.”
And then Paul turns toward the person doing the judging.
The trap closes.
The moral spectator discovers that he, too, is standing in the courtroom.
And by Romans 3 the verdict becomes universal:
All have sinned.
Nobody gets to swagger toward the cross.
Nobody arrives carrying a résumé.
Nobody walks into Calvary saying, “Jesus, You are fortunate to have me.”
We crawl there empty-handed.
Gay or straight.
Religious or rebellious.
Church-raised or completely lost.
Sexually broken or secretly proud.
Addicted.
Greedy.
Self-righteous.
Bitter.
Lustful.
Jealous.
Dishonest.
Ashamed.
Every one of us needs mercy.
That does not mean every sin is identical in its earthly consequences.
It means every sinner ultimately needs the same Savior.
And this is where Christians can make a catastrophic mistake with Romans 1.
We can defend biblical sexual ethics and somehow forget biblical grace.
Truth without love becomes a weapon.
But what our culture calls “love” cannot require Christians to erase whatever Scripture says simply because obedience becomes socially expensive.
Jesus gives us something better than either cowardice or cruelty.
Grace and truth.
So if you experience same-sex attraction, hear this carefully.
You are not a punchline.
You are not a political talking point.
You are not beyond the reach of Jesus Christ.
And experiencing temptation is not itself permission for another Christian to treat you with contempt.
Christian discipleship calls every believer—not merely one particular group—to bring desires, identities, relationships, ambitions and bodies underneath the lordship of Christ.
For one disciple, surrender may touch sexuality.
For another, pornography.
For another, adultery.
For another, greed.
For another, pride.
For another, resentment that has been fermenting for twenty years.
For another, the desperate addiction to being admired.
Different battles.
Same throne.
The Christian question eventually becomes:
Who gets to be Lord?
That is why the Gospel cannot end with, “Stop sinning.”
If Christianity were merely God shouting moral instructions down from heaven at people incapable of saving themselves, none of us would have hope.
The Gospel announces something infinitely greater.
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
The sinless Son of God entered our ruin.
He bore sin.
He endured the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
And now forgiveness is not offered to people who successfully pretend they never became dirty.
Forgiveness is offered through Christ to people who repent and believe.
That means the church should be one of the few places on earth where someone can finally stop pretending.
Imagine a man sitting silently in the back of a church.
He has followed Jesus for years.
But there is a struggle he has never told anyone about.
He is terrified.
Not merely because of what he feels.
Because he knows what Christians sometimes do with confessions.
So he sings.
He smiles.
He shakes hands.
He says, “I'm doing good.”
And inside he is exhausted.
Maybe your hidden battle is completely different.
But you understand the sentence:
“If they really knew me…”
If they knew what you watched.
If they knew what you wanted.
If they knew what happened.
If they knew how angry you were.
If they knew what you did after midnight.
If they knew how many times you promised God it was the last time.
If they knew how empty your marriage feels.
If they knew what your mind has been entertaining.
If they knew how far you wandered.
Listen.
The Gospel does not say your sin is imaginary.
It says your sin does not have to write the final chapter.
That is radically different.
Jesus does not save us by convincing us darkness is light.
He saves us by entering our darkness and bringing us into His light.
Repentance is therefore not God saying, “Clean yourself up enough and maybe I'll love you.”
Repentance is the sinner finally releasing the thing that is killing him because he has discovered Someone infinitely better.
Jesus.
This is why we cannot rewrite Romans 1 to make Christianity easier.
But neither can we stop at Romans 1 and pretend condemnation is the climax of Paul's Gospel.
Keep reading Romans.
There is justification.
Peace with God.
Grace.
Freedom from condemnation.
Adoption.
The Spirit.
Hope.
Mercy.
Transformation.
And eventually that staggering promise that nothing can separate God's people from the love of God in Christ Jesus.
The Bible's story is not:
“Look at those disgusting sinners.”
It is:
Look at the holiness of God. Look at the rebellion of humanity. And then look at the astonishing mercy of Jesus Christ.
That is where Romans 1 should eventually drive us.
Not toward hatred.
Toward the cross.
Not toward self-congratulation.
Toward repentance.
Not toward pretending sin does not matter.
Toward the Savior who died because it matters terribly—and who rose because sin and death do not get the final word.
So perhaps the most dangerous way to read Romans 1:27 is to read it thinking only about somebody else.
Maybe your struggle is not theirs.
Fine.
What is yours?
What desire have you been protecting from Jesus?
What relationship have you declared off-limits to His authority?
What secret appetite keeps negotiating with your conscience?
What idol would devastate you if Christ asked you to surrender it?
What sin have you renamed because repentance would cost too much?
Don't answer publicly unless you genuinely want to.
But answer God.
Because there is a frightening difference between struggling against sin and making peace with it.
Somebody reading this has been fighting privately for months.
Maybe years.
You fell again.
You prayed again.
You wondered whether Jesus was tired of hearing your voice.
And perhaps tonight you need to remember:
The answer to your shame is not better hiding.
It is coming into the light of Christ.
Repentance does not mean you will never experience another battle.
It means you have stopped calling the enemy your king.
So come home.
Not when you become impressive.
Now.
Come with trembling hands.
Come ashamed.
Come exhausted.
Come confused.
Come carrying the parts of your story you wish could be erased.
Jesus already knows what is in the room.
And the cross is still standing.
Not because a comment saves anyone.
Christ saves.
But sometimes the first crack in hiding is finally admitting that you need Him.
Someone else reading the comments may desperately need to discover that they are not the only Christian fighting a private war.
If someone came to mind while you were reading this, don't use this article as a weapon against them.
Love them.
Pray for them.
And if sharing it would genuinely help them encounter Scripture and the Gospel rather than merely make them feel targeted, send it with compassion.

But voluntary support of Gospel ministry is biblical. Paul himself speaks appreciatively of believers partnering with him in giving and receiving, and the New Testament repeatedly presents Christian generosity as willing rather than coerced.
You cannot purchase God's favor.
You cannot donate enough to erase yesterday.
Salvation is not merchandise.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Pray.
Send it privately to someone searching for answers.
Because somewhere tonight there is another person staring at a screen while fighting a battle nobody knows exists.
Maybe this article reaches them because you shared it.
Maybe they finally pray.
Maybe they finally confess.
Maybe they finally open Romans and discover that the chapter they thought existed merely to condemn somebody actually belongs to a letter announcing God's power to save sinners.
And maybe, eventually, they discover the truth every redeemed person must discover:
The worst chapter of your life does not have to become the last chapter of your life.
Because when Jesus takes the pen, even the chapter you were ashamed to let anyone read can become the place where grace begins writing something new.
